description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Indian Judiciary (FDA & SDA Examination Notes). Covers Supreme Court, High Courts, Subordinate Courts, Judicial Review, Judicial Activism, Writs, and Independence of Judiciary.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Part of the Constitution deals with the Union Judiciary?

options.B: Part V, Chapter IV

questions.explanation: Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124 to 147 deals with the Union Judiciary.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Part of the Constitution deals with High Courts in the States?

options.B: Part VI, Chapter V

questions.explanation: Part VI, Chapter V, Articles 214 to 231 deals with High Courts in the States.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Articles deal with subordinate courts?

options.B: Articles 124 to 147

questions.explanation: Articles 233 to 237 in Part VI, Chapter VI deal with subordinate courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the broad structure of the Indian judicial system?

options.A: A dual system with separate federal and state courts
options.B: An integrated hierarchy consisting of the Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts at the State or regional level, and subordinate district and lower courts
options.C: Only Supreme Court and High Courts
options.D: A three-tier system with independent state supreme courts

questions.explanation: The Indian judicial system is an integrated hierarchy with the Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts at the State/regional level, and subordinate district and lower courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is meant by an integrated judicial system?

options.A: Separate court systems for Union and States
options.B: The Supreme Court, High Courts and subordinate courts form one hierarchy administering both Union and State laws
options.C: Only one court for the entire country
options.D: Judiciary is integrated with the legislature

questions.explanation: An integrated judicial system means the Supreme Court, High Courts and subordinate courts form one hierarchy administering both Union and State laws, rather than separate federal and State court systems.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article establishes the Supreme Court of India?

options.B: Article 124

questions.explanation: Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court of India.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides for High Courts for States?

options.B: Article 214

questions.explanation: Article 214 provides for High Courts for States.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article permits a common High Court for two or more States or States and Union Territories?

options.B: Article 231

questions.explanation: Article 231 permits a common High Court for two or more States or States and Union Territories.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides for appointment of district judges?

options.B: Article 235

questions.explanation: Article 233 provides for appointment of district judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides for High Court control over subordinate courts?

options.B: Article 234

questions.explanation: Article 235 provides for High Court control over subordinate courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What are the main functions of the judiciary?

options.B: Interpreting and applying laws, resolving disputes, protecting rights, reviewing government action and ensuring that public authorities act within constitutional limits

questions.explanation: The main functions of the judiciary include interpreting and applying laws, resolving disputes, protecting rights, reviewing government action and ensuring that public authorities act within constitutional limits.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Does India follow an absolutely rigid separation of powers?

options.B: No, the Constitution provides functional separation with checks and balances
options.C: Yes, but only between judiciary and legislature
options.D: No, there is no separation at all

questions.explanation: India does not follow an absolutely rigid separation of powers. The Constitution provides functional separation with checks and balances, rather than a watertight separation.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: When was the Supreme Court of India inaugurated?

options.B: 28 January 1950

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which institution preceded the Supreme Court of India?

options.B: Federal Court of India

questions.explanation: The Federal Court of India, established in 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935, preceded the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Where did the Supreme Court initially function?

options.B: In the Chamber of Princes in the Parliament House building

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court initially functioned in the Chamber of Princes in the Parliament House building; it moved to its present building in 1958.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court?

options.B: Article 124

questions.explanation: Article 124 deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who appoints Supreme Court judges under the Constitution?

options.B: The President of India

questions.explanation: The President of India appoints Supreme Court judges through the constitutionally applicable appointment process as interpreted by the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What are the constitutional qualifications for appointment as a Supreme Court judge?

options.A: Must be an Indian citizen and at least 35 years old
options.B: Must be an Indian citizen and must have been a High Court judge for at least five years, or an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years, or be a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion
options.C: Must be an Indian citizen and must have been a High Court judge for at least ten years
options.D: Must be an Indian citizen and must have been an advocate for at least five years

questions.explanation: The person must be an Indian citizen and must have been a High Court judge for at least five years, or an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years, or be a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the retirement age of a Supreme Court judge?

options.B: 62 years

questions.explanation: The retirement age of a Supreme Court judge is 65 years.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the retirement age of a High Court judge?

options.B: 62 years

questions.explanation: The retirement age of a High Court judge is 62 years.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who administers the oath to a Supreme Court judge?

options.B: The President or a person appointed by the President

questions.explanation: The President or a person appointed by the President administers the oath to a Supreme Court judge.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can a Supreme Court judge resign?

options.B: Yes, the judge may submit a signed resignation addressed to the President
options.C: Yes, but only with Parliament's approval
options.D: Yes, but only after 10 years of service

questions.explanation: Yes, a Supreme Court judge may submit a signed resignation addressed to the President.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: On what grounds can a Supreme Court judge be removed?

options.B: Proved misbehaviour or incapacity

questions.explanation: A Supreme Court judge can be removed on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the constitutional procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge?

options.A: Simple majority in both Houses of Parliament
options.B: Each House of Parliament must pass an address in the same session supported by a majority of its total membership and at least two-thirds of members present and voting; the President then issues the removal order
options.C: The President can remove a judge by executive order
options.D: The Supreme Court can remove a judge by its own resolution

questions.explanation: Each House of Parliament must pass an address in the same session supported by a majority of its total membership and at least two-thirds of members present and voting; the President then issues the removal order.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Articles govern removal of Supreme Court judges?

options.B: Article 124(4) and Article 124(5), together with the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968

questions.explanation: Article 124(4) and Article 124(5), together with the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, govern removal of Supreme Court judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Is the word 'impeachment' used in the Constitution for removal of judges?

options.A: Yes, it is the official term used
options.B: No, the Constitution uses the term 'removal'; impeachment is commonly used informally
options.C: Yes, but only for Supreme Court judges
options.D: Yes, but only for High Court judges

questions.explanation: The Constitution uses the term removal; impeachment is commonly used informally.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can a judge's salary and allowances be reduced to the judge's disadvantage after appointment?

options.A: Yes, by Parliament at any time
options.B: No, except during a Financial Emergency as constitutionally permitted

questions.explanation: A judge's salary and allowances cannot be reduced to the judge's disadvantage after appointment, except during a Financial Emergency as constitutionally permitted.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who determines the sanctioned number of Supreme Court judges?

options.B: The Chief Justice of India

questions.explanation: Parliament by law determines the sanctioned number of Supreme Court judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in specified Union-State and inter-State disputes?

options.B: Article 131

questions.explanation: Article 131 provides the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in specified Union-State and inter-State disputes.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is original jurisdiction?

options.A: Power to hear appeals from lower courts
options.B: The power to hear a matter at first instance, rather than on appeal
options.C: Power to review its own judgments

questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction is the power to hear a matter at first instance, rather than on appeal.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides appeals to the Supreme Court in constitutional matters?

options.B: Article 132

questions.explanation: Article 132 provides appeals to the Supreme Court in constitutional matters.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides appeals in civil matters to the Supreme Court?

options.B: Article 133

questions.explanation: Article 133 provides appeals in civil matters to the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides appeals in criminal matters to the Supreme Court?

options.B: Article 133

questions.explanation: Article 134 provides appeals in criminal matters to the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides Special Leave to Appeal?

options.B: Article 134

questions.explanation: Article 136 provides Special Leave to Appeal.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is a Special Leave Petition (SLP)?

options.A: A petition for writ of habeas corpus
options.B: A request asking the Supreme Court to exercise its discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from a judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order
options.C: A petition for review of a Supreme Court judgment

questions.explanation: An SLP is a request asking the Supreme Court to exercise its discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from a judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order, subject to constitutional exclusions.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article gives the Supreme Court power to review its judgments or orders?

options.B: Article 137

questions.explanation: Article 137 gives the Supreme Court power to review its judgments or orders.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides the President's power to seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion?

options.B: Article 142

questions.explanation: Article 143 provides the President's power to seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Is an advisory opinion under Article 143 ordinarily binding on the President?

options.B: No, it is advisory, though it has substantial constitutional and persuasive value
options.C: Yes, but only if accepted by Parliament
options.D: It is binding only in criminal matters

questions.explanation: An advisory opinion under Article 143 is advisory, though it has substantial constitutional and persuasive value.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article declares the Supreme Court a court of record?

options.B: Article 129

questions.explanation: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a court of record.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What powers follow from the Supreme Court being a court of record?

options.A: Only the power to hear appeals
options.B: Its records have evidentiary value and it can punish for contempt of itself

questions.explanation: As a court of record, the Supreme Court's records have evidentiary value and it can punish for contempt of itself.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India?

options.B: Article 141

questions.explanation: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice?

options.B: Article 142

questions.explanation: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article requires civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court?

options.B: Article 142

questions.explanation: Article 144 requires civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to make rules regulating its practice and procedure?

options.B: Article 143

questions.explanation: Article 145 empowers the Supreme Court to make rules regulating its practice and procedure.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article enables Parliament to enlarge the Supreme Court's jurisdiction?

options.B: Article 138

questions.explanation: Article 138 enables Parliament to enlarge the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is a Constitution Bench?

options.A: A bench of three Supreme Court judges
options.B: A bench of at least five Supreme Court judges constituted to decide a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, or for other constitutionally specified purposes
options.C: A bench of seven High Court judges
options.D: A bench constituted only for criminal appeals

questions.explanation: A Constitution Bench is a bench of at least five Supreme Court judges constituted to decide a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, or for other constitutionally specified purposes.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article requires at least five judges to decide a substantial question of constitutional interpretation?

options.B: Article 145(3)

questions.explanation: Article 145(3) requires at least five judges to decide a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the difference between original and appellate jurisdiction?

options.A: Original jurisdiction hears appeals; appellate jurisdiction hears matters first
options.B: Original jurisdiction hears a matter first; appellate jurisdiction reviews a decision made by a lower court or tribunal
options.D: Original jurisdiction is only for criminal matters

questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction hears a matter first; appellate jurisdiction reviews a decision made by a lower court or tribunal.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?

options.A: A proceeding initiated by the government only
options.B: A proceeding initiated to protect public interest or the rights of persons who may be unable to approach a court themselves
options.C: A proceeding only for criminal cases
options.D: A proceeding only for constitutional amendments

questions.explanation: PIL is a proceeding initiated to protect public interest or the rights of persons who may be unable to approach a court themselves.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which courts can entertain PILs?

options.B: Only High Courts
options.C: The Supreme Court under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226, subject to jurisdiction and procedural rules

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226 can entertain PILs, subject to jurisdiction and procedural rules.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which judges are strongly associated with the development of PIL in India?

options.A: Justices M. Hidayatullah and S. R. Das
options.B: Justices P. N. Bhagwati and V. R. Krishna Iyer
options.C: Justices Y. V. Chandrachud and P. N. Bhagwati
options.D: Justices A. K. Sikri and D. Y. Chandrachud

questions.explanation: Justices P. N. Bhagwati and V. R. Krishna Iyer are strongly associated with the development of PIL in India.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is locus standi?

options.A: The power of the court to punish for contempt
options.B: The legal standing or entitlement of a person to bring a matter before a court
options.C: The power of the Supreme Court to review its judgments
options.D: The power of the President to appoint judges

questions.explanation: Locus standi is the legal standing or entitlement of a person to bring a matter before a court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Why was traditional locus standi relaxed in PIL cases?

options.A: To reduce the burden on courts
options.B: To improve access to justice for disadvantaged groups and address public wrongs where directly affected persons may be unable to approach courts
options.C: To increase government control over courts
options.D: To limit the number of cases filed

questions.explanation: Traditional locus standi was relaxed in PIL cases to improve access to justice for disadvantaged groups and address public wrongs where directly affected persons may be unable to approach courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can any person file any case as a PIL merely by claiming public interest?

options.A: Yes, anyone can file any case as PIL
options.B: No, courts examine bona fides, public injury, maintainability and whether the matter is genuinely in public interest
options.C: Yes, but only in the Supreme Court
options.D: Only government officials can file PILs

questions.explanation: Courts examine bona fides, public injury, maintainability and whether the matter is genuinely in public interest before entertaining a PIL.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides for a High Court for each State?

options.B: Article 214

questions.explanation: Article 214 provides for a High Court for each State.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can one High Court serve more than one State?

options.A: No, each State must have a separate High Court
options.B: Yes, Article 231 permits Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States or States and Union Territories
options.C: Yes, but only with the consent of the Supreme Court
options.D: Yes, but only for Union Territories

questions.explanation: Article 231 permits Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States or States and Union Territories.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article deals with the constitution of High Courts?

options.B: Article 216

questions.explanation: Article 216 deals with the constitution of High Courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who appoints High Court judges?

options.B: The Chief Justice of the High Court
options.C: The President of India under Article 217

questions.explanation: The President of India appoints High Court judges under Article 217, through the constitutionally applicable appointment process as interpreted by the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What are the constitutional qualifications for appointment as a High Court judge?

options.A: Must be an Indian citizen and at least 35 years old
options.B: Must be an Indian citizen and must have held judicial office in India for at least ten years or been an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years
options.C: Must be an Indian citizen and must have been a district judge for at least five years
options.D: Must be an Indian citizen and must have been a law professor for at least ten years

questions.explanation: The person must be an Indian citizen and must have held judicial office in India for at least ten years or been an advocate of a High Court (or two or more such courts in succession) for at least ten years.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article deals with appointment and conditions of office of High Court judges?

options.B: Article 216

questions.explanation: Article 217 deals with appointment and conditions of office of High Court judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article deals with transfer of a High Court judge?

options.B: Article 218

questions.explanation: Article 222 deals with transfer of a High Court judge.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who transfers a High Court judge?

options.A: The Chief Justice of the High Court
options.B: The Governor of the State
options.C: The President, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India

questions.explanation: The President transfers a High Court judge, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides for additional and acting High Court judges?

options.B: Article 224

questions.explanation: Article 224 provides for additional and acting High Court judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article permits retired High Court judges to sit and act as judges?

options.B: Article 224A

questions.explanation: Article 224A permits retired High Court judges to sit and act as judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Is the removal procedure for High Court judges different from that for Supreme Court judges?

options.A: Yes, High Court judges have a simpler removal procedure
options.B: No, Article 218 applies the Supreme Court judge removal procedure to High Court judges
options.C: Yes, High Court judges can be removed by the Governor
options.D: Yes, High Court judges can be removed by the Chief Justice

questions.explanation: No, Article 218 applies the Supreme Court judge removal procedure to High Court judges.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article gives High Courts power to issue writs?

options.B: Article 226

questions.explanation: Article 226 gives High Courts power to issue writs.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Is Article 226 wider than Article 32 in subject matter?

options.A: No, both are identical in scope
options.B: Yes, Article 226 permits writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose; Article 32 is specifically for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
options.C: No, Article 32 is wider than Article 226
options.D: Yes, but only for criminal matters

questions.explanation: Article 226 permits writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose; Article 32 is specifically for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article declares a High Court a court of record?

options.B: Article 215

questions.explanation: Article 215 declares a High Court a court of record.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article gives High Courts superintendence over courts and tribunals within their territory?

options.B: Article 227

questions.explanation: Article 227 gives High Courts superintendence over courts and tribunals within their territory, subject to constitutional limitations.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article gives High Courts control over district and subordinate courts?

options.B: Article 228

questions.explanation: Article 235 gives High Courts control over district and subordinate courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article provides for transfer of certain cases to a High Court where a substantial constitutional question is involved?

options.B: Article 227

questions.explanation: Article 228 provides for transfer of certain cases to a High Court where a substantial constitutional question is involved.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article permits extension of a High Court's jurisdiction to Union Territories?

options.B: Article 228

questions.explanation: Article 230 permits extension of a High Court's jurisdiction to Union Territories.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the territorial jurisdiction of a High Court?

options.B: The State or States and Union Territories for which it is constituted or whose jurisdiction is extended by law
options.C: Only the capital city of the State
options.D: Only the district where it is located

questions.explanation: The territorial jurisdiction of a High Court is the State or States and Union Territories for which it is constituted or whose jurisdiction is extended by law.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can High Courts review the constitutionality of State and Union laws?

options.A: No, only the Supreme Court can do so
options.B: Yes, subject to constitutional limits and the jurisdiction of constitutional courts
options.C: Yes, but only for State laws
options.D: Yes, but only for Union laws

questions.explanation: High Courts can review the constitutionality of State and Union laws, subject to constitutional limits and the jurisdiction of constitutional courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can a High Court decision be appealed to the Supreme Court?

options.A: No, High Court decisions are final
options.B: Yes, where the Constitution or applicable law provides an appeal, or where the Supreme Court grants special leave under Article 136
options.C: Yes, but only in criminal matters
options.D: Yes, but only with the President's permission

questions.explanation: A High Court decision can be appealed to the Supreme Court where the Constitution or applicable law provides an appeal, or where the Supreme Court grants special leave under Article 136.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Articles deal with subordinate courts?

options.B: Articles 124 to 147

questions.explanation: Articles 233 to 237 deal with subordinate courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who appoints district judges?

options.B: The Chief Justice of the High Court
options.C: The Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to that State, under Article 233

questions.explanation: The Governor of the State appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to that State, under Article 233.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What minimum advocacy experience is required for direct recruitment as a district judge under Article 233(2)?

options.A: At least three years as an advocate or pleader
options.B: At least five years as an advocate or pleader
options.C: At least seven years as an advocate or pleader, along with recommendation by the High Court
options.D: At least ten years as an advocate or pleader

questions.explanation: At least seven years as an advocate or pleader, along with recommendation by the High Court, is required for direct recruitment as a district judge under Article 233(2).

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Who appoints persons to the State judicial service other than district judges?

options.B: The Chief Justice of the High Court
options.C: The Governor under Article 234, in accordance with rules made after consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court

questions.explanation: The Governor appoints persons to the State judicial service other than district judges under Article 234, in accordance with rules made after consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What does High Court control under Article 235 include?

options.B: Posting, promotion and grant of leave to persons in the State judicial service holding posts inferior to district judge, subject to constitutional provisions

questions.explanation: High Court control under Article 235 includes posting, promotion and grant of leave to persons in the State judicial service holding posts inferior to district judge, subject to constitutional provisions.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article enables application of the subordinate-courts chapter to certain magistrates?

options.B: Article 234

questions.explanation: Article 237 enables application of the subordinate-courts chapter to certain magistrates.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the usual civil court hierarchy below a High Court?

options.A: It is uniform across all States
options.B: It varies by State, but commonly includes District Judge, Additional District Judge, Civil Judge (Senior Division) and Civil Judge (Junior Division)

questions.explanation: The civil court hierarchy below a High Court varies by State, but commonly includes District Judge, Additional District Judge, Civil Judge (Senior Division) and Civil Judge (Junior Division).

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What are the principal criminal courts under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?

options.B: Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the First Class and Second Class, and Executive Magistrates

questions.explanation: The principal criminal courts under the BNSS, 2023 are Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the First Class and Second Class, and Executive Magistrates, subject to the statutory framework and special courts.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for new criminal procedure from 1 July 2024?

options.B: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS)

questions.explanation: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for new criminal procedure from 1 July 2024, subject to commencement and savings provisions.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the role of a District and Sessions Judge?

options.B: Only criminal jurisdiction
options.C: The officer heads the district-level judiciary; as District Judge the officer exercises civil jurisdiction and as Sessions Judge exercises criminal jurisdiction under applicable law

questions.explanation: The District and Sessions Judge heads the district-level judiciary; as District Judge the officer exercises civil jurisdiction and as Sessions Judge exercises criminal jurisdiction under applicable law.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Are tribunals identical to ordinary subordinate courts?

options.B: No, tribunals are specialised adjudicatory bodies created under constitutional provisions or statutes, though their decisions remain subject to constitutional judicial review
options.C: Yes, but only in criminal matters
options.D: No, tribunals are not subject to judicial review

questions.explanation: Tribunals are not identical to ordinary subordinate courts. They are specialised adjudicatory bodies created under constitutional provisions or statutes, though their decisions remain subject to constitutional judicial review.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is judicial review?

options.A: The power of the legislature to review court decisions
options.B: The power of constitutional courts to examine the constitutionality and legality of legislative, executive and other public actions and invalidate them when they violate the Constitution
options.C: The power of the President to review court decisions
options.D: The power of the Supreme Court to review its own judges

questions.explanation: Judicial review is the power of constitutional courts to examine the constitutionality and legality of legislative, executive and other public actions and invalidate them when they violate the Constitution.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Article declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency?

options.B: Article 13

questions.explanation: Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which Articles empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs respectively?

options.B: Articles 226 and 32

questions.explanation: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court and Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What are the purposes of judicial review?

options.A: To increase the power of the legislature
options.B: To uphold constitutional supremacy, protect Fundamental Rights, maintain federal limits and ensure that public authorities act within legal powers
options.D: To make the judiciary supreme over the Constitution

questions.explanation: The purposes of judicial review include upholding constitutional supremacy, protecting Fundamental Rights, maintaining federal limits and ensuring that public authorities act within legal powers.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is the difference between judicial review and appeal?

options.B: Judicial review examines legality or constitutionality; an appeal permits reconsideration of a decision within the scope of appellate law
options.C: Judicial review is only for criminal cases; appeal is for civil cases
options.D: Appeal examines constitutionality; judicial review examines facts

questions.explanation: Judicial review examines legality or constitutionality; an appeal permits reconsideration of a decision within the scope of appellate law.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Can constitutional amendments be judicially reviewed?

options.A: No, constitutional amendments are immune from review
options.B: Yes, an amendment may be reviewed to determine whether it damages or destroys the Constitution's basic structure
options.C: Yes, but only for procedural irregularities
options.D: Yes, but only with the President's consent

questions.explanation: Constitutional amendments can be judicially reviewed to determine whether they damage or destroy the Constitution's basic structure.

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: Which case established that Parliament cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution through amendment?

questions.question: Why was traditional locus standi relaxed in PIL cases?

questions.question: What is judicial review?

questions.question: What is the difference between judicial review and appeal?

questions.question: Can constitutional amendments be judicially reviewed?

options.A: No, constitutional amendments are immune from review
options.B: Yes, an amendment may be reviewed to determine whether it damages or destroys the Constitution's basic structure

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is constitutional supremacy?

questions.question: What may happen when a law is declared unconstitutional?

questions.subject: Indian Polity
questions.question: What is judicial activism?

options.C: An approach where courts defer to the legislature

questions.question: Is judicial activism expressly defined in the Constitution?

questions.question: How does judicial activism differ from judicial review?
